title: Redwood cost econ discovery w/ Falcon Quant
summary: Discovery focused on per-token unit economics and levers (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization, dedicated vs hosted). Falcon Quant has a constrained monthly budget, wants realistic cost modeling for a 1k-5k daily user workload and a plan for a short pilot to benchmark latency/cost tradeoffs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 09:12 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Eleanor Wu (CTO, Falcon Quant), Samir Patel (Head of ML Ops), Liam O'Connor (VP Eng), Renee Jacobs (Finance)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving time, uh this is Maya from Redwood, with me is Carlos our solutions engineer. Quick round robin?
[00:10] Eleanor Wu: yeah hi Eleanor here, CTO, quick note - we're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for our inference, mostly cost and latency concerns.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir here. We run a lot of short-run inference for trading insights, so tail latency matters.
[00:24] Carlos Rivera: mm-hmm, got it. Real quick - are you primarily concerned with per-token operating cost, or the upfront committed costs for reserved clusters?
[00:33] Liam O'Connor: both. Finance wants a predictable monthly number, but engineering cares about p99 latency under load. We have a hard cap of about $35k/mo for inference initially.
[00:42] Renee Jacobs: yes budget is the blocker, and we'd need a clear cost model to justify moving to dedicated.
[00:47] Maya Chen: perfect - that's what we'll focus on. Can you share current traffic profile? average tokens per request, qps, that kind of thing?
[00:55] Eleanor Wu: rough numbers: 1k users/day, avg 3 completions per user, each completion is about 250 tokens in and 150 tokens out. Peak qps maybe 80 during market open, average 8-12 qps.
[01:12] Carlos Rivera: thanks. Okay, starting from Redwood hosted: per-token pricing gives you low ops overhead and you pay per usage. We typically quote x per prompt token and y per completion token - (note: pricing callouts often rough in conversation). With your numbers that maps to roughly 1.2M tokens/month, ballpark.
[01:34] Samir Patel: 1.2M, got it. How much does batching help in hosted? we can't change workload shape much.
[01:40] Carlos Rivera: batching helps primarily on throughput-heavy workloads. For your qps profile, continuous batching gains are modest except if you buffer a few 10s of ms. Also prefix/KV caching is the big lever when many requests share a similar prompt prefix - that can reduce repeat compute.
[01:56] Liam O'Connor: we do have a lot of shared prompt context; like top-of-book market context is identical across many requests, only the user id or small prompt differs.
[02:05] Maya Chen: that sounds ideal for KV / prefix caching - in Redwood you can cache encoder outputs and reuse the KV cache to cut generated-token compute. Quantization is another lever: lower-bit quant models reduce GPU cost per token, though slight quality delta.
[02:20] Eleanor Wu: What's the delta typically - in like 8-bit vs 4-bit?
[02:24] Carlos Rivera: 8-bit quant is a safe sweet spot for many open models with minimal quality loss; 4-bit can be more aggressive and sometimes needs evals. Cost wise you can see 20-40% per-token improvements moving from fp16 to 8-bit, and further from 8-bit to 4-bit but with diminishing returns and more risk.
[02:45] Samir Patel: ok so caching + 8-bit is our baseline. How does that translate to monthly cost under hosted vs dedicated?
[02:52] Maya Chen: rough example - hosted per-token gets you flexibility, but unit cost is higher. For predictions: hosted might put you around $0.0008-0.0012 per generated token depending on model and caching. Dedicated with reserved fleet can drop unit cost substantially - sometimes 40-60% lower depending on utilization and instance types. But you take on committed monthly cost.
[03:16] Renee Jacobs: committed cost worries me - we don't know if usage will grow above 2k users. What's a minimal dedicated commit we could start with?
[03:24] Carlos Rivera: typically customers start with a single-node reserved pool (e.g., 1-2 A100-equivalent GPUs) for a pilot. That gives predictable throughput and lets us run a cost amortization model. We can model expected tokens/month vs throughput SLOs.
[03:39] Liam O'Connor: can you run a quick amortization example now with our 1.2M tokens?
[03:44] Maya Chen: sure. If hosted is ~ $0.001 per output token (conservative) your monthly would be about $1,200 just for generated tokens - plus prompt tokens maybe another $900 - so around $2.1k - wait that's off - let me recalc: 1.2M tokens total at $0.001 -> $1,200 yes, but we need to split prompt vs generated. With your input/output split it's closer to 720k prompt tokens and 480k output tokens; so total cost at $0.0008 prompt / $0.001 generation is about $576 + $480 = $1,056. I think I'm missing a decimal here, sorry, math typo -
[04:12] Eleanor Wu: sounds like you were low earlier - our expectation from other vendors was $15k-20k/mo, which is why we're cautious.
[04:20] Carlos Rivera: yep there's always model choice and pricing variance. Also many vendors include additional platform fees. We'll send a detailed cost spreadsheet. The key point: hosted is easy and may be cheaper short term for low volume, dedicated lowers marginal unit cost as you scale.
[04:36] Samir Patel: what about caching savings? Say 40% of responses hit the prefix cache - how to model that?
[04:42] Maya Chen: you can model effective tokens = raw_tokens * (1 - cache_hit_rate). If 40% of tokens are saved on the generation side, that directly reduces generated token cost. Also batching can reduce per-token latency cost slightly by improving throughput per GPU.
[04:58] Liam O'Connor: any native tooling to estimate cache hit rate?
[05:02] Carlos Rivera: Redwood Console shows token-level breakdowns, cache hit rates, and per-route stats. For a POC we instrument a week of traffic to estimate realistic cache hit % and batching opportunities.
[05:13] Renee Jacobs: security check - we need SOC2, KMS, SSO (SAML), and audit logs. Also must ensure data residency in us-east for now.
[05:22] Maya Chen: Redwood supports SOC2, KMS integrations, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and you can pin deployment region. For Dedicated/Private we offer customer-managed KMS and VPC peering.
[05:33] Eleanor Wu: good. On the pilot - can we start hosted but with ability to migrate to dedicated without re-architecting?
[05:40] Carlos Rivera: absolutely that's one of Redwood's strengths - same API across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and model pinning so you can roll traffic to a dedicated fleet without code changes.
[05:50] Samir Patel: latency - p99 under 300ms is our target for single-turn completions. Is that achievable with caching?
[05:57] Carlos Rivera: yes for short responses with KV cache we often hit p50 50-100ms and p99 sub-300ms depending on model and region. For long-gen workloads p99 rises. We'll include baseline SLO numbers in the follow-up.
[06:10] Liam O'Connor: competitor question - we also looked at self-hosting with Triton and cloud providers like Vertex AI. How does Redwood compare cost-wise?
[06:18] Maya Chen: self-hosting has lower unit infra cost but higher ops and reliability overhead. Vertex AI pricing can be competitive for certain models but may lack the inference-specific levers Redwood provides like fine-grained KV caching, automatic prefix caching, and unified rollouts. We'll put a comparison table in the doc.
[06:33] Renee Jacobs: what's the minimum POC timeline and cost?
[06:36] Carlos Rivera: typically 2-3 weeks: week 1 instrument traffic and share prompts, week 2 run benchmarks and tune batching/caching/quant settings, week 3 review results and decide next steps. Cost for Redwood-led benchmarking is usually covered as part of pilot discussions; if you want dedicated reserved nodes for a week there may be a nominal pass-through. We'll detail in email.
[06:55] Eleanor Wu: ok sounds good. For the benchmarking we will share sanitized prompt corpus and traffic slice.
[06:59] Maya Chen: perfect. We'll also include a simple amortization workbook showing hosted vs dedicated vs private at different utilization levels and cache-hit assumptions.
[07:07] Samir Patel: one more technical - how does fallback work if dedicated pool saturates?
[07:12] Carlos Rivera: Redwood has smart routing: you can set fallback to hosted or to a spare burst pool. That way you protect latency-sensitive flows while keeping costs controlled.
[07:23] Liam O'Connor: thanks. Any gotchas we should know about with model quantization and evals?
[07:28] Carlos Rivera: always run quality evals with representative prompts. Sometimes 4-bit needs small prompt engineering tweaks; we recommend 8-bit for initial runs.
[07:37] Renee Jacobs: ok finance sign-off will require a clear expected monthly spend range. Can you provide low/medium/high scenarios?
[07:43] Maya Chen: yes - we'll return a low/medium/high cost table factoring in cache hit rates 10/30/50% and utilization 30/60/90%.
[07:53] Eleanor Wu: great. Should we schedule the scoping follow-up?
[07:56] Maya Chen: how's next Tuesday 10am your time?
[07:58] Eleanor Wu: works for me.
[08:00] Liam O'Connor: works here.
[08:02] Maya Chen: ok we'll send invite. Quick recap and action items now.
[08:06] Carlos Rivera: recap: we'll run amortization and cost spreadsheet, plan a 2-3 week pilot, include measurements for caching and batching and potential dedicated commit sizes. We'll share security docs and SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[08:18] Renee Jacobs: thanks, please include pricing scenarios so finance can review.
[08:22] Maya Chen: absolutely. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the workbook and an invite.
[08:27] Eleanor Wu: thanks all, bye.

Note: transcription contains a few math corrections and verbal hesitations, minor mis-heard product names possible (eg "Redwood dedicate"), typical of auto-transcripts.
